sections.title: Paris events
sections.content:
• Guitar Travellers at 38Riv — today, 19:30 or 21:30. 38Riv Jazz Club, 38 rue de Rivoli, Paris 4e. Malo Athouël, Baptiste Renou and Mathis Cordier play an all-guitar trio built from original compositions with folk, jazz and blues influences. Each set lasts an hour. €19–22 online; €22–25 at the door; reservation advised. Ville de Paris
  • Les Arènes Lyriques — today, 21:00–22:30. Arènes de Montmartre, 25 rue Chappe, Paris 18e. A 15-player orchestra plus the second-session soloists — soprano Anara Khassenova, tenor Jérémie Schütz, soul vocalist Laurine Moullet and pianist Alexandre Lombard-Buffet — in a programme deliberately crossing opera, orchestral repertoire and soul. Announced anchors include Márquez's Danzón No. 2, Puccini's Nessun dorma, Catalani's La Wally and Nina Simone. €45 full / €34 reduced. It is outdoors; if weather forces a move, the concert can be transferred to Saint-Jean de Montmartre. Official site · Ticket information
  • “Aux origines — Regards croisés sur le racisme et les discriminations” — today, 10:00–17:30. Palais de la Porte Dorée, 293 avenue Daumesnil, Paris 12e. The temporary exhibition combines contemporary art with social-science research on discrimination attached to real or perceived origin. It runs only until 23 August, so this is a reasonable last-two-weeks option rather than something to leave indefinitely on the list. €12 full / €9 reduced; free for under-26s. Exhibition page

sections.title: CS and AI developments
sections.content:
Learned image compression that treats packet loss as a representation problem

A new paper, Every Packet Counts, starts from a practical failure mode that learned image codecs often under-model: the latent representation is not equally important everywhere, and entropy models can create long sequential dependencies. Lose the wrong packet and the decoder can therefore lose both unusually important information and context needed to decode later information.

The proposed codec attacks both problems inside the representation. Inter-Channel Redistribution spreads latent energy more evenly across channels before packetisation; Interleaved Channel Grouping then distributes strided channel groups across packets rather than leaving locally concentrated information together. The entropy model is also changed to a two-layer dual-branch autoregressive structure, shortening the dependency chain so one missing packet is less able to poison what follows.

At 20% packet loss, the authors report an average +1.84 dB PSNR over LossResilientLIC and about an order-of-magnitude reduction in PSNR variance. Training with uniformly random losses also transfers to burstier Gilbert–Elliott losses in their experiments. The systems point is more interesting than the headline number: if the transport layer is unreliable, robustness can be designed into where information lives and how decoding depends on it, rather than being left entirely to retransmission or external FEC. Paper

Attribute hallucinations can come from weak visual evidence, not an overactive language prior

A second new paper, VISOR, tests a common explanation for VLM hallucination: that the language model's prior overwhelms the image. The authors use a null-image diagnostic to decompose the output logit into a visual signal and a language-prior signal, then examine 10,791 negative-ground-truth samples across three VLM families and three attribute classes.

The surprising result is that the visual signal strongly predicts false positives, while the language-prior component is near chance in this setup. The errors then split into two mechanisms. For colour/state, the visual direction is often broadly correct but the margin is too small, so the model overcommits to uncertain evidence. For material, the visual signal is more often low-SNR or misaligned with the correct attribute.

That distinction changes the intervention. A low-margin colour judgment calls for calibration or abstention; a systematically misaligned material representation suggests targeted visual adaptation. Simply suppressing the language prior would be aimed at the wrong subsystem. It is a useful mechanistic diagnostic because it turns “hallucination” from one umbrella error into failure modes with different fixes. Paper

sections.title: Technical idea: rank/select lets a bit vector behave like a navigable set
sections.content:
Suppose a sorted set of integers is represented implicitly as a bit vector B: position i is 1 exactly when i belongs to the set. Two operations make this much more useful than a raw bitmap:

  • rank1(i) asks how many 1-bits occur up to position i;
  • select1(j) asks where the j-th 1-bit occurs.

With only those operations you can translate between a dense ordinal — “the 43rd present item” — and its sparse universe position, or count how many stored values lie before a point. Succinct indexes, compressed text structures, graph representations and bitmap-heavy databases use this constantly.

A practical rank structure does not rescan from the beginning. It stores cumulative counts at coarse superblocks, smaller counts inside each superblock, then finishes the last machine word with hardware popcount. select can sample positions of every k-th 1 and search or scan only within the resulting small region. More sophisticated structures give constant-time operations with sublinear auxiliary space.

The design pattern is the useful part: store the underlying set in the cheapest representation, then add a very small navigation index rather than materialising a second array of integer positions. It is one of the ideas behind succinct data structures: auxiliary metadata can recover rich query semantics without giving up the density advantage of a bitmap. Engineering survey

sections.title: Non-CS science: a dismantled German fission plant is becoming fusion infrastructure
sections.content:
At Biblis, one of the German nuclear plants shut after Fukushima, the startup Focused Energy is trying an unusual route to laser fusion: reuse an old fission site rather than begin with an empty field. The company raised €210 million in May, including €60 million from site owner RWE. Construction is already creating a clean room where lasers are scheduled to begin installation in 2027, with a prototype reactor targeted for 2035.

Focused Energy follows inertial-confinement fusion: many powerful lasers compress a tiny fuel capsule until temperature and density are sufficient for fusion. The important precedent is the US National Ignition Facility's 2022 shot, which produced more fusion energy than the laser energy delivered to the target. That is not the same thing as a commercial plant producing net electricity after accounting for laser inefficiency, repetition rate, target manufacturing, thermal conversion and the rest of the facility.

So the interesting part today is not “fusion solved.” It is the industrialisation hypothesis. Biblis already has grid connections, an energy-industry workforce, land, safety institutions and a utility owner accustomed to very large power infrastructure. If fusion physics does become commercially usable, those surrounding assets may shorten deployment just as much as another improvement inside the target chamber. The 2035 date remains a startup roadmap, not a demonstrated power-plant schedule. Le Monde

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• Russia and Syria are replacing the old basing arrangement with a thinner negotiated footprint. Moscow and Damascus signed a memorandum after about 18 months of talks: Syria is to regain civilian control of Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartous, while military facilities are to become joint training centres within three months. A Syrian source says some Russian forces will remain. The material compromise is clear: Damascus gets a visible restoration of sovereignty while Russia preserves some Mediterranean logistics and training access without the same enclave-like base structure it held under Assad. Reuters
  • The US–Iran bargaining space is widening in a way that makes agreement harder. Gulf markets fell Tuesday as optimism about a deal and full restoration of Strait of Hormuz shipping weakened after Washington added demands for compensation tied to past US losses from wars, attacks and protests. Adding a second distributive dispute to nuclear/security bargaining creates more questions over valuation, sequencing and who concedes first. Markets can price that increased probability of delay before negotiators formally declare talks dead. Reuters
  • North Korea launched another missile this morning ahead of the US–South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises. South Korean and Japanese authorities say the projectile flew about 700 km from the Wonsan area; Seoul has not yet definitively classified the weapon. It is the 11th suspected ballistic-missile test of 2026 by South Korean accounting. The timing, days before the 17–27 August exercises, makes signalling against the drills a plausible interpretation, but the weapon type and Pyongyang's own stated purpose remain unresolved. Reuters
  • Venezuela and Israel have resumed consular services after a 17-year diplomatic break. This stops short of full diplomatic restoration, which is precisely why it matters as an institutional step: consular relations restore practical state-to-state functions and can test a political opening without immediately committing either government to embassies and full normalization. In Venezuela's broader post-Maduro foreign-policy realignment, it is a relatively cheap and reversible signal compared with a treaty or strategic partnership. Reuters

sections.title: Marxist fragment: Engels on clearing a slum without abolishing the housing relation
sections.content:
“they are not abolished; they are merely shifted elsewhere!”

— Friedrich Engels, The Housing Question, Part II. Primary text

Engels is describing the nineteenth-century Haussmann-style method: demolish crowded working-class districts where they become politically, commercially or aesthetically inconvenient and drive the displaced population elsewhere. His claim is not that every street improvement is fake or every redevelopment necessarily worsens housing. It is that removing a bad physical stock does not remove the economic process that recreates overcrowding when low-income households still have to compete for scarce housing under the same property and income relations.

That is a useful causal distinction. An urban policy can genuinely improve sanitation, transport and buildings at the cleared site while simultaneously exporting the housing pressure. If the diagnosis is only “these blocks are bad,” demolition looks like a complete solution; if the diagnosis includes rents, wages, land values and replacement supply, relocation becomes part of the model rather than an accidental side effect.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
Burke: conservation requires a capacity to revise

“A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.”

— Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France. Primary text

This is a more interesting Burke than the caricature of conservatism as “never change anything.” His argument is that a political order unable to correct damaged parts becomes brittle enough to endanger the parts worth preserving. The tension is between correction inside an inherited structure and reconstruction from abstract first principles. You can reject Burke's defence of hierarchy while retaining the institutional point: systems sometimes need controlled mutability precisely because invariance is not the same thing as stability.

Paine: society and government solve different coordination problems

“Society is produced by our wants, and government by our wickedness”

— Thomas Paine, Common Sense, 1776. Primary text

Paine sharply separates voluntary social cooperation from coercive political authority. People associate because exchange, affection and mutual dependence are productive; government appears because conflict, predation and rule-breaking make some coercive restraint necessary. That gives political authority a burden of justification: useful social order does not by itself prove that a particular government, office or inherited power produced it.

Put beside Burke, the disagreement becomes cleaner. Burke asks how to preserve accumulated institutions while making enough repairs for them to survive. Paine asks which parts of social life need political authority at all, and therefore which inherited powers have to justify their existence rather than borrowing legitimacy from society's spontaneous cooperation.

sections.title: French usage: dernier carat
sections.content:
Dernier carat is a familiar, slightly old-school way to mean the absolute latest point / the final deadline. The Académie française defines le dernier carat figuratively as l'extrême limite.

  • Envoie-moi ça lundi, dernier carat. — Send me that Monday at the latest.
  • Je dois partir à 18 h, dernier carat. — I absolutely have to leave by six.
  • On se décide demain, dernier carat. — We decide tomorrow, no later.

It is more idiomatic and marked than neutral au plus tard. In formal writing, au plus tard lundi or la date butoir est lundi will normally be cleaner; in conversation, dernier carat adds a “hard stop, really no later than this” flavour. Académie française

sections.title: Music corner
sections.content: Three direct recommendations. Open the three-video YouTube queue.

items.label: Classical
items.piece: Mozart — Don Giovanni, K. 527: Deh! vieni alla finestra
items.performer: Thomas Allen; Academy of St Martin in the Fields; Sir Neville Marriner
items.description: 2:08. A deliberate form change: a compact operatic serenade rather than another instrumental miniature or late-Romantic orchestral work. The attraction is the unusually clean melodic line and economical accompaniment — Mozart gets a complete lyrical character into barely two minutes. This is also a useful test of whether the melodic/coherent classical preference transfers to voice-led opera rather than only instrumental repertoire.

items.label: Jazz
items.description: 2:32. Solo piano from Piano Improvisations Vol. 1 (1971): short, harmonically rich and foreground-oriented without the polished fusion production of yesterday's Dan Siegel hit. The recommendation is less about another jazz pianist than about seeing whether Corea's compact melodic improvisation lands when there is nowhere for the writing to hide behind ensemble texture.

items.label: Other
items.description: 4:45. A move into trip-hop: a persistent harpsichord-like figure, restrained beat and Elizabeth Fraser's floating vocal line create a piece whose repetition is carried by timbral and harmonic tension rather than by a big structural build. Since repetitive electronic material has sometimes landed as merely background music, this is a sharper test: the loop is extremely stable, but the song has a much stronger melodic identity than the recent BICEP miss.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: Maya Blue is an ancient organic–mineral composite
sections.content:
The vivid blue surviving on Maya murals and objects is not simply a mineral pigment. Maya Blue combines indigo — an organic dye — with palygorskite, a fibrous clay mineral. The resulting clay–organic complex is unusually resistant to acids, alkalis and tropical weathering, which is why the colour can remain recognizable centuries later.

The material-science trick is that palygorskite is not an inert powder that merely dilutes the dye. Its nanoscale channels and surfaces host and constrain indigo molecules, changing the dye's chemical environment and shielding it from reactions that would more readily destroy free indigo. Heating the mixture is part of the traditional preparation routes studied experimentally, helping create the stable hybrid structure.

There is also archaeological evidence connecting the pigment to actual clay sources. Comparative mineral analyses of Maya Blue from Chichén Itzá and Palenque matched palygorskite from mines still known to Maya communities, giving direct evidence that those source traditions extend back at least seven centuries. So a pre-Columbian pigment achieved something recognisably modern in materials terms: combine an organic chromophore with an inorganic host to obtain properties neither component has alone. USGS / Journal of Archaeological Science

sections.title: Puzzle / dilemma: Newcomb’s problem
sections.content:
A nearly infallible predictor has already examined you and filled two boxes:

  • Box A is transparent and contains $1,000.
  • Box B is opaque. If the predictor predicted that you would take only B, it put $1,000,000 inside. If it predicted that you would take both A and B, it left B empty.

The prediction is finished and the boxes are now fixed. You may either one-box — take only B — or two-box — take both.

The two arguments are both unpleasantly strong:

  • Dominance: whatever is already in B, taking A as well gives you exactly $1,000 more. So take both.
  • Expected payoff: the predictor is extremely reliable, so people who take only B almost always find $1,000,000, while people who take both almost always get only $1,000. So take only B.

Your present action cannot causally travel backwards and refill Box B. But your action is extremely strong evidence about what the earlier prediction was. The puzzle is therefore not really about psychic powers; it asks what rational choice should optimise when causal influence and evidential correlation point in opposite directions.

What do you take? Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
